privacyIntro: This policy describes the current {appName} application and website. {appName} is an open source project operated by {operatorName}.
privacyLocalBody: The current version of {appName} runs on your device and stores the configuration and session data it manages locally. {appName} does not upload your code, conversations, or usage data to servers operated by {operatorName}.
privacyAgentsTitle: Agents and tools from other providers
privacyAgentsBody: {appName} starts the third-party coding agents you configure. These agents and their tools may send prompts, code, context, and other data to their service providers according to your configuration and actions. Their providers’ privacy policies and terms apply to that processing. Repository operations may also connect to the Git remotes you configure, including when checking remote status.
privacySharingBody: To coordinate work, task descriptions, reports, and relevant context pass between participating sessions. When this information enters another agent's session, it may be processed by that agent's configured provider. Working with agents from different providers may therefore involve sharing task information with multiple providers.
privacyContactTitle: Information you choose to send us
privacyContactBody: If you contact us by email or through GitHub Issues, we receive the information you choose to provide and use it to respond to your request. Information posted in a public issue is visible to others. For privacy questions, contact {operatorName} at the email address below.

faqSetupQuestion: Do I need to set up my projects and CLI configuration again?
faqSetupAnswer: Add your existing project folder without moving your code. The default account uses your existing CLI configuration, and the agent still loads your project's instructions, skills, hooks, and MCP servers. Additional accounts use separate configurations, with optional sharing of supported settings.
faqSubagentsQuestion: Why not develop every project in one session, or have one agent use subagents?
faqProvidersQuestion: Can each project keep an agent from a different provider?
faqParticipationQuestion: How do projects report back, and can I step in?
faqParticipationAnswer: A requirement or code detail may be easier to explain directly to the project agent doing the work. You can enter its conversation to add context, adjust requirements, or review code; sessions started by the coordinator still report results, open items, and decisions needed back to it.
developerTitle:
Let AI write the code.
Put your energy into the product.
developerIntro: I built {appName} because I believe people no longer need to write code by hand. Developers can put their attention back where it matters: the product they want to deliver.
developerShiftBody: As AI produces more code, reviewing and rewriting every line by hand can no longer keep pace. I see the shift toward implementation happening inside a black box as irreversible. In my view, AI already writes more complete logic than most programmers. The conventions for “good code” that we designed around human readers are losing their central role as AI takes on both writing and maintenance.
developerContextBody: I see the biggest obstacle in AI development as misunderstanding: unclear requirements, missing context, or assumptions left unstated. The work that deserves our attention is defining the problem, explaining constraints, and giving agents the context they need to work toward the same goal.
developerQualityBody: For me, software quality has one deciding standard: whether the product meets real needs under thorough testing. Reading code cannot establish that on its own. Tests need to cover real workflows, edge cases, and failures, and their results need to guide the next iteration.
developerPurpose: That is the purpose of this workspace: coordinating agents, carrying context forward, and following the work through to delivery. As developers spend less time in code editors, they can devote more of it to requirements, decisions, testing, and the product itself.
developerInvitation: If you also believe people no longer need to write code themselves, this workspace is built for you.

workspaceIntroduction: Bring your existing coding agents and accounts into one development workspace. Switch accounts within the same agent while keeping the conversation, or hand work to an agent from another provider. Choose an agent to coordinate tasks across your projects.
coordinationWalkthroughDescription: Take a meal promotion across a restaurant’s ordering, payment and store-management projects. The illustration below shows a coordinator assigning tasks and receiving reports. Select a project to see its assigned task and example report.
faqSetupCostsAnswer: Install and configure the coding-agent command-line tools you want to use first. {appName} is free and open source under the MIT License; agents and model services follow the subscriptions or billing terms of the providers you choose. If your agent supports a self-hosted model, you can keep using that configuration too.
faqDataFlowAnswer: {appName} keeps its application data locally and does not upload your code or conversations to its own servers. Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build use services you subscribe to or configure, with your own accounts; these tools manage account credentials and conversation records. They send prompts, code and relevant context to the providers you configure, under those providers’ policies. When agents collaborate, task descriptions, progress and relevant context also pass to the agents taking part.
faqParallelWorkAnswer: Sessions share the project folder by default, so simultaneous edits to the same file can conflict. For parallel work, ask the agents to use separate Git worktrees and review the changes before merging.
faqCliResumeAnswer: Yes. Project files stay in their original folders and each agent keeps its own conversation records. While the original agent still has a conversation record, you can resume that conversation through its command-line tool. With an extra account, start the tool using that account’s configuration directory.
consentBody: May we use Google Analytics to understand how this website is visited? It sets cookies and sends usage data to Google. Google Analytics is not loaded unless you allow it.
featurePreviewError: The interface example could not load. Reload the page to try again.
faqProjectIsolationAnswer: Developing several projects in one session can mix their contexts. Working across directories or using subagents does not guarantee that the target project’s full configuration is loaded: rules can be missed when the parent session has to pass them on, and loading behavior varies by tool. {appName} starts an independent native session of the chosen agent in each project directory, so the agent loads local configuration through its own mechanisms while the coordinator organizes the work.
faqAgentChoiceAnswer: Yes. Choose Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build independently for the coordinator and each project, based on the task and the project’s tools. Each agent keeps its own instructions and toolchain, while {appName} passes tasks, relevant context and reports between sessions. The coordinator can delegate work and bring the results together.
privacyWebsiteConsentBody: This is a static website hosted on GitHub Pages. We use a cookie to remember the language selected or detected for this browser for one year. We use Google Analytics to understand website visits only with your consent. It uses cookies and sends usage data to Google. If you decline before allowing it, Google Analytics is not loaded. We remember your choice in a cookie for one year. You can change it through “Analytics settings” in the site footer. If you withdraw consent after allowing analytics, we stop sending further analytics data from that page and remove its Google Analytics cookies. GitHub records visitors’ IP addresses for security purposes; see GitHub’s privacy statement.
downloadLinuxDescription: Install octoboardd, the {appName} daemon, on a Linux server without root. Reach it from the macOS or Windows app, or from a browser over SSH.
downloadLinuxRange: For x86_64 and aarch64, on any distribution.
heroAvailability: macOS on Apple silicon and Intel · Windows on x64 · Linux server on x86_64 and aarch64 · Beta
workspaceSeoSummary: Manage Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build accounts in one open source workspace for macOS and Windows, plus a Linux server. Track usage, switch accounts and coordinate coding agents across projects.
faqRemoteHostsAnswer: Yes. Run agents on your Linux server or on another Mac or Windows PC running {appName}. Connect to that machine over SSH from the desktop app or a browser.
privacyRemoteHostsBody: When you connect over SSH to a Linux server or another computer you manage, agent sessions run and their data stays on that host. The interface travels over your SSH connection without a relay. The desktop app stores your saved remote daemons and any downloaded copies locally. It keeps its device’s private SSH key in the macOS login keychain or Windows Credential Manager and adds the public key to the remote user’s authorized_keys on the host. It does not store your SSH password.
downloadServiceSteps: To install it as a systemd user service that starts right away, replace the final {plain} with {option}, and add {port} for another port. The script then turns on lingering, so the service keeps running after you log out and starts at boot; if it says it could not, run {linger} once (it may need sudo).
downloadUpgrade: To upgrade, run the install command again, then {restart}.
downloadPathNote: If the install says {binDir} is not on your PATH, run {start} by the full path it prints, or add {binDir} to your PATH.
downloadSeoTitle: Download {appName} for macOS, Windows and Linux
downloadSeoDescription: Download the {appName} app for macOS or Windows, or install its Linux server with one command. Free and open source under the MIT License.
downloadMacosRequirements: For Apple silicon and Intel Macs, on macOS 11 or later.
downloadWindowsRequirements: For x64, on Windows 10 version 21H2 or later. On Windows 11 on Arm, the x64 app runs under emulation. The installer downloads Microsoft Edge WebView2 if it is missing, which needs an internet connection.
downloadWindowsSmartScreen: The app is not code-signed yet, so Microsoft Defender SmartScreen may show “Windows protected your PC”. Select “More info”, then “Run anyway”.
downloadUpdates: Later versions arrive through the app’s own updates.
downloadTeaser: Get the macOS or Windows app, or install the Linux server with one command.

downloadDemoLocalCaption: On your own machine: forward the port, then open the address in a browser.

downloadPortNote: The default port is {defaultPort}; use {port} to change it. {address} prints an SSH command using your server details, for example {forward}.

processMonitoringFeatureTitle: See what your agents leave running.
processMonitoringFeatureDescription: See processes started by agents, their memory, listening ports and local web links in real time. When a session ends, Octoboard tries for a limited time to stop the processes it tracked and you haven’t chosen to keep.
openAgentAppFeatureTitle: Pick up a session in the Claude or Codex app.
openAgentAppFeatureDescription: Open a stopped session in its agent’s app on the Mac or Windows PC running the daemon.
sharedConfigurationFeatureDescription: Accounts of the same agent can share skills, plugins and MCP servers. Claude Code’s user-level MCP servers stay separate. On Windows, enable Developer Mode on the daemon host.
remoteIntro: Use the macOS or Windows app to work on a Linux server or another computer through SSH, an encrypted connection straight to that machine, with no relay or cloud service.
remoteStepInstallBody: Sign in to the server over SSH as the user who’ll run {appName}, then run this command to install its background service without administrator access.
remoteStepStartBody: Start the background service so the desktop app has something to connect to.
remoteStepDetailsBody: Run this command on the server and copy the line beginning with {connectionScheme}, which tells the app where and how to connect.
remoteAddressOverride: If this computer reaches the server at a different address or SSH port, add {host} or {port} to the command to print the right connection details.
remoteQr: The QR code contains the same line. No client scans it yet.
remoteStepConnectBody: Open {remoteLabelDevices} from the app’s rail or, on macOS, choose {remoteLabelMenuDevices} from the menu. Select {remoteLabelAdd}, use {remoteLabelPaste} in {remoteLabelDetails}, and choose {remoteLabelPassword} or {remoteLabelKeyFile}. Select {remoteLabelSave} and then {remoteLabelConnect} to open a separate window.
remoteWindowsMenu: On Windows, you can also choose {remoteLabelWindowsDevices} from the window’s system menu or the taskbar icon’s jump list.
remoteFingerprint: Pasting details that include a host fingerprint saves it automatically. If you entered the host by hand, compare the fingerprint shown at first connection with the server’s before confirming. For a Linux server’s Ed25519 host key, run {fingerprintCommand} on the server.
remoteHostTitle: Use another computer as the host
remoteHostSsh: On the computer you want to reach, follow the system settings link in {settingsPath} and turn on {remoteLabelLogin} on macOS or {remoteLabelOpenSsh} on Windows so it accepts SSH sign-ins.
remoteHostAllow: Turn on {remoteLabelAllow} and leave the app running so it can accept connections from your other computer.
remoteHostDetails: Copy {remoteLabelDetails} from the {remoteLabelAppTab} tab to tell your other computer where to connect.
remoteBrowserCommand: Get the command that carries your browser’s traffic to the host over SSH from the host app’s {remoteLabelBrowserTab} tab, or run {addressCommand} on Linux to print it.
remoteBrowserServer: For a Linux server, replace {server} in the printed SSH command with the address your computer uses to reach the server.
remoteBrowserOpen: Once the command is running, open the browser address shown alongside it.
remoteBrowserKey: Only someone who can reach Octoboard through the SSH forward can use this address. Keep it private: its key grants full control and is saved with the address in browser history and bookmarks, including when they sync.
remoteSecuritySsh: Octoboard only accepts connections from the host itself, so to connect from another computer you first need to sign in to the host over SSH.
remoteSecurityHost: The app remembers the host key, the machine’s SSH identity, on the first successful connection and blocks the connection with an alert if that identity later changes.
remoteSecurityDevice: After you first sign in with a password or your own key file, the app sets up a separate SSH key for this computer to use for future sign-ins.
remoteSecurityRevoke: Remove that computer’s entry from the host’s list of allowed SSH keys ({authorizedKeys} on Linux and macOS) to block new sign-ins with that key while leaving any open connection in place until it ends.
remoteWindowWork: Each connected combination of user, host and SSH port has its own window with its own projects, sessions and notifications.
remoteWindowMenu: Open the app’s menu bar icon on macOS or its notification-area icon on Windows to see a tab for each connection.
remoteWindowWeb: When you click a {localhost} link to a website an agent started on the host, the app carries the browser’s traffic to that website over SSH.
remoteWindowFiles: View a file in the remote window or download a copy to open in this computer’s default app for that file.
remoteWindowReconnect: If the network drops, the window keeps trying to reconnect until it gets through or you close it.
remoteHostConnect: On the computer you’ll work from, follow step 4 of the Linux instructions above to add the host using the details you copied.
remoteBrowserRun: Run the SSH command in a terminal on the computer where you’ll use the browser and leave it running while you work.
accountContinuityFeatureDescription: Switch accounts of the same agent and continue the conversation, manually or with automatic switching at the usage limit.
quotaSchedulingFeatureTitle: Let available quota decide when work runs.
quotaSchedulingFeatureDescription: Automatically pick an available account for new sessions. With automatic switching on, a task with no eligible account waits and resumes after a fresh reading confirms recovery.
freshSessionFeatureTitle: Start fresh before the context fills up.
freshSessionFeatureDescription: Check context usage when the agent reports it and start the next stage in a fresh session. Revisit the earlier conversation while its record is available.
crossProjectWorkFeatureTitle: One request. Coordinate work across projects.
crossProjectWorkFeatureDescription: Give one request to a coordinator that assigns work to the agents for each project, follows progress and brings their reports together.
nativeProjectSessionsFeatureTitle: Each project keeps its own setup.
nativeProjectSessionsFeatureDescription: Work in separate native CLI sessions that load each project’s instructions, skills, hooks and MCP configuration.
sessionInterventionFeatureTitle: See which sessions need you. Step in directly.
sessionInterventionFeatureDescription: See which sessions are working or waiting, then open the project session to answer a question or adjust instructions directly.
